I couldn't finish this. My search and fetch tools hit their limit partway through, so these notes cover only part of what you asked for. I fully read one source, the Enduring Word page for the whole chapter. The rest comes from search-result extracts that gather the old commentaries, and these were fullest for vv. 1–5 and 15. I never reached any page for parts 2 and 3: none of the tradition-specific sites, netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, the Catholic or Orthodox sites, or anything on prosperity or hyper-grace teaching. Wherever a verse is missing a kind of note below, it's because I didn't find it.

## 1. Traditional reading, verse by verse

**vv. 1–2:** Guzik says God is speaking to Judah about breaking the old covenant made at Mount Sinai under Moses (Exod 24). He quotes Harrison: God promised to meet the nation's needs in return for worship of Him alone and obedience. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-11/
- Kingcomments: King Josiah's revival changed people outwardly but not inwardly, so Jeremiah has to remind them of the covenant. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/jeremiah-11.html
- The BibleHub study page links the chapter to the "Book of the Law" found in the temple around 622 BC. It says the people's response was keen but shallow, and their zeal had cooled by now. https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/jeremiah/11.htm

**v. 3:** Guzik says the curse points back to the curses for breaking the covenant in Deut 27:15–26. He quotes Trapp's guess that Jeremiah may have been holding the book of Deuteronomy as he spoke. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-11/

**v. 4:**
- Guzik: the "iron furnace" picture appears three times in Scripture (here, Deut 4:20 and 1 Kings 8:51). Some think it may refer to actual iron furnaces where the Israelite slaves worked. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-11/
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: "furnace" stands for the severe testing and "iron" for how long it lasted. Barnes: the furnace is Egypt itself. Poole: it could be literal slave work or a figure for very hard labour. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/11-4.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch: the covenant made in Moab was a renewal of the Sinai covenant, which is why it is linked to the Exodus. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/11-4.htm
- Matthew Henry (Concise): applied to today, forgiveness is offered freely, but no one is saved who refuses God's command to repent, believe in Christ and turn from sin. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/11-4.htm
- Benson: God's rescue put the people under obligation before He gave the law. A furnace refines metal, which fits Israel's long suffering in Egypt. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/11-4.html
- Chuck Smith: obedience is "the condition." https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/smith_chuck/c2000_jer/jer_011.cfm

**v. 5:**
- Guzik: God kept His side by giving them a good land, and it was Israel that failed. He quotes Meyer praising Jeremiah's "Amen" as an example, and Morgan contrasting a heartfelt Amen with an empty ritual one. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-11/
- Barnes and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: Jeremiah is doing exactly what Deut 27:14–26 commands and agreeing that the curses are just. Ellicott links the Amen to the people's covenant renewal under Josiah (2 Kings 23:3). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/11-5.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: "As it is this day" is a phrase from Deuteronomy that points to what the people could see for themselves. The Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) translates the Amen as "may it be so." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/11-5.htm
- Clarke reads it as "let Your promises be fulfilled, and let the stubborn beware of Your warnings." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/11-5.html
- Matthew Henry compares the covenant to a lease: obedience was the rent, and God had the right to take the land back if it went unpaid. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/jeremiah/11.htm

**vv. 6–8:** Guzik: Jeremiah has to preach this message all over Judah. God's "rising early" is a figure of speech for how hard He worked to warn them, and the people followed their own hearts instead. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-11/
- Matthew Henry: God keeps track of how long we have had the means of grace and how often we have been warned. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/jeremiah/11.htm

**vv. 9–10:** Guzik suggests the "conspiracy" may have been organised by spiritual forces even if the people didn't know it. He also quotes Thompson, who calls it a figure of speech for an apostasy that looked like a planned plot, and Harrison, who says the Canaanite fertility cults spread so widely it seemed deliberate. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-11/

**vv. 11–13:** Guzik: the disaster is the penalty the Mosaic covenant promised. The false gods will be silent because they are nothing, while the LORD will be silent as a judgment. He calls God's silence in a time of trouble one of the worst curses there is. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-11/

**v. 14:**
- Preacher's Homiletical Commentary: forbidding prayer for the people (v. 14) goes with refusing their sacrifices (v. 15). It says no prayer can be heard for people who love their sin. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/jeremiah-11.html
- Matthew Henry: people who have put themselves beyond God's hearing can't count on other people's prayers either. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/11-16.html

**v. 15:**
- Guzik: Israel is the "beloved" acting like an unfaithful wife. "When you do evil, then you rejoice" describes a sin-sick society. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-11/
- On BibleHub's v. 15 page (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/11-15.htm):
  - Ellicott: the Hebrew is hard and probably damaged, but the general point is clear: ritual on its own cannot save.
  - Barnes compares Isa 1:12. Public worship of the LORD doesn't fit with private immorality and idolatry.
  - Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: the sacrifices had stopped being holy and acceptable to God. It quotes Horsley picturing Judah as a priest's adulterous wife who has lost her share of the sacrifice.
  - Poole: the sacrifices were spoiled because they were offered to idols as well as to God.
  - Benson gives another reading: the priests' share of the sacrifices would end because the temple would be destroyed.
  - Pulpit and Keil & Delitzsch prefer "Shall vows and holy flesh remove your calamity?"

**vv. 16–17:** Guzik: the olive-tree name shows how tenderly God loved them, and that love does not cancel judgment on stubborn idolatry. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-11/
- Matthew Henry: every sin against God is also a sin against ourselves. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/jeremiah/11.htm

**vv. 18–19:** Guzik: God protected Jeremiah by revealing the plot of the men of Anathoth, his home town. The "docile lamb" recalls Jesus, rejected by His own people and called a lamb in Isa 53:7. He quotes Harrison that a man's enemies will be those of his own household. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-11/
- Preacher's Homiletical Commentary: the picture is of a tame pet lamb that was later slaughtered. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/11-1.html

**v. 20:** Guzik: Jeremiah responded the right way, by praying. He asked for protection based on God's righteousness and left vengeance to God (Deut 32:35; Rom 12:19). He quotes Kidner: the prayer may shock us, but it asks no more than justice. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-11/

**vv. 21–23:**
- Guzik: Anathoth's priests may have resented Josiah closing their local shrine, and Jeremiah supported Josiah. He quotes Thompson's comparison with families today who turn on a relative they think has disgraced them. The threat shows it was God's message they hated. He suggests Jeremiah probably had mixed feelings about the judgment, and he quotes Clarke that it would come through the sword and famine of the Babylonian invasion. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-11/
- Pulpit Commentary (homiletics): the persecution was murderous, and silencing the prophet was really refusing God's message. Jeremiah was soon vindicated, while God had put up with wrongs against Himself for centuries. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-11.html

## 2. Where Protestant traditions differ

I found no pages from the traditions' own sites, so I can't report real differences between traditions. The nearest thing is that individual older commentators disagree on v. 5:
- Calvin: Jeremiah said the Amen in his own name because he knew the people would resist. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/11-5.html
- Matthew Henry: Jeremiah agrees either for himself or on the people's behalf. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/jeremiah/11.htm
- Chuck Smith (labelled Calvary Chapel/Dispensational on StudyLight) links it to the Amens shouted at Mount Ebal. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/11-5.html

## 3. Other views (only what I found)

- **v. 4:** The Cambridge Bible thinks "and do them" probably slipped in by mistake from v. 6. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/11-4.htm
- **v. 5:** Coffman argues against "radical critics" who say only a fragment of Deuteronomy existed in Jeremiah's day. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/11-5.html
- **v. 15:**
  - Ellicott mentions a guessed correction of the text based on the Septuagint. The Cambridge Bible adopts the Septuagint's "fat pieces" (of sacrifices). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/11-15.htm
  - Gill reports Jewish readings: Kimchi takes the holy flesh as godly men who had died, Jarchi takes it as neglected circumcision, and the Targum talks of mixing unclean meat with holy. Cocceius reads the "beloved" as Christ leaving the temple. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/11-15.htm
  - The Catholic Douay-Rheims Bible translates the verse "shall the holy flesh take away from thee thy crimes," but this is only a translation, not commentary. https://biblehub.com/esv/jeremiah/11-15.htm

Once the tools are available again, the next places to look are netbible.org notes on vv. 15 and 19, preceptaustin.org, and the BibleHub verse pages for vv. 9–23.
